Q: Difference between User and System Installer of Visual Studio Code A:

The good old PoLP... Visual Studio Code is from a trusted publisher but extensions that are installed can come from 3rd parties and aren't guaranteed to be trustworthy so running them as admin (SYSTEM user) could be even more +catastrophic if you fuck up (we all do). I'll give a couple scenarios where your choice would be something worth considering:

Per-user install:

You're at home, you're the only person who logs into your machine and your user has admin rights already... No real need for installing as SYSTEM user/admin and its a smarter choice just in case.

or maybe

You're at a business where you don't manage their IT systems, your PC might be shared with others, or you don't have admin permissions given by your company but still have basic permissions to work with...

System install

Let's say you're at home, have multiple accounts that you use (for different aliases/other purposes) you might not want to download the same extensions or tools again on each account.... Or speculation, you might have a small company with no DC (domain controller) or serious business IT infrastructure.... You might have a small team that you want the same tools available to them when you/they log into the PC....

or maybe

You're in a large company, but many users share a machine. Or lets say, you have private tools/extensions (for anything, not just VS Code) and installing system-wide makes much more sense to save an individual user having a misconfiguration of their software - which might or might not cause big problems when what they produce turns out different to what the company expects....

------------------------------------------------------------

I doubt I've given a definitive answer on the "best" option, because what's best for me isn't necessarily the best option for you. Hope I've given you or other readers a bit of insight at least

Q: Why do static const declaration within class and inline constexpr definition outside class work together A:

constexpr isn't a type. It pertains to the initializer of the variable for which it's declared. That's why it can only appear in definitions (only definitions have initializers). constexpr also implies const which is why const is needed at the declaration.

Q: How can I print a dynamic Tic Tac Toe board in C++ without hardcoding values? A:

you see how you use numbers to indicate which index you want from that list to be used to print it out? I want you to use two for loops; One for each row, and for each of those rows, there should be another for loop to display that specific row's columns. When getting the values for each individual box, you can do board[row][column]. And also, when using a loop when using cout<<... you dont necessarily need to use endl to go to the next row, this is useful for your column printing (you will do this in a loop and use an "cout<<endl" at the end of that for loop). now keep in mind, if you want to seperate a rectangle into 2, you divide it with 1 line; for 3, 2 lines; for 4 sections, 3 lines... so n-1 amount of lines. So just print a "|" after each column except the last one. And for your case, you wouls also want to print "-------" after each row, except the last one.
Now since you are new, I also want you to assign the "player" an int of 0, and XOR (^) it with 1 each time you want to change players. I want you to to be curios about stuff like this too for you to dive deeper. And for you projects further cases, you can implement a "check_if_finished()" function to use after every single time someone makes a move. so "make_a_move()" function would be called with x (column) and y (row) value to make a place an X or an O depending whether the player is a 0 or 1, call "check_finished()" right after that to print out the current player and declare it the winner; if its not the winner, simply XOR that with 1 and make your "make_a_move()" loop keep going. you can figure out all of the boxes being filled to call it a draw yourself. Good luck!

Q: InteractiveBrokers API: an instrument's market state? A:

Indeed, it seems there is nothing to check if a market is open/closed.

I'm currently relying on getting the book (bid/ask).

A closed market will have:

  1. Bid/ask readings to be 0 (one or both of them).
  2. Bid will equal ask (more common).

By validating the book, you can get a grasp of what is being traded out there.
Obviously, it is not bulletproof, as a market can have a circuit breaker on.

Also note that requesting historical data is not enough, as a market can be open for trading, but without any trades traded so far (zero volume).
